newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bund strips draw institutions, retail investors shy.
newsitem.headline: Bund strips draw institutions, retail investors shy.

text.p: Stripping is swiftly coming into vogue in Germany's bond market, but private retail investors are proving to be less enthusiastic than their institutional counterparts.

Market strategists say the Bonn government's timing in introducing strippable bonds a month ago was favourable for large players, and it will only be a matter of time before the fashion takes hold with smaller-scale investors.

"When you have a situation where debt markets are strong anyway, this type of product adds liquidity and is a useful way to take advantage of the longer maturities," said Sonja Gibbs, economist at Nomura in London.

Bond stripping -- already common in the United States, France, Belgium and the Netherlands -- allows the coupon, or fixed income, element of a bond to be stripped from the principal amount and the two parts to be traded separately.
With German debt yields falling as the market rallies, investors are increasingly looking for ways to lengthen the duration and maturity of their bond portfolios.

Demand for Germany's 30-year long bond, which is particularly attractive for stripping because it offers the longest principal duration, has been markedly higher since stripping was launched in Germany on July 1.

With buyers so eager, analysts say it was a liquidity squeeze on the 10- and 30-year bonds which on Friday prompted the Bundesbank to top up the two issues by two billion marks each to 19 billion and 12 billion marks respectively.
The demand has also pushed yields sharply lower at the long end of the market.

Coupled with a sell-off at the short end sparked by concern the Bundesbank might be forced to tighten rates to support the falling deutschemark, this has produced some of the most dramatic flattening of the yield curve seen this year.
"(The Bund strips market) is attracting insurance companies and long-term pension funds as well as some retail individuals," said Paul Walters, also at Nomura in London.
Analysts said the big players in this new market were international traders -- mainly from France -- seeking to make money through arbitrage between French and German debt strips.
So far, with strips being a relatively new, niche product, interest among the more cautious German retail investors has been slight, but this demand too is soon likely to pick up.
"The first flows from retail investors were very thin," said Christian Schaller, fixed income strategist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Frankfurt.
But he said this was mainly due to a lack of marketing.

"In the medium-term, when one of the retail banks starts marketing the advantages of strips -- and there are many advantages for the retail sector -- private investors will be an important group in this market," said Schaller.

The main benefit of strippable bonds for retail investors is that tax penalties which would normally be levied on annual or bi-annual coupon payments are avoided, while the final tax liability is pushed forward to the bond's maturity date.
For investors nearing retirement, for example, investing in a stripped 10-year bond means the final capital return will taxable at somewhat lower pensioners' rates.
Nomura's Walters said another area of potentially large growth in strips would be the domestic pension fund industry.

"The pension fund industry is not particularly well developed in Germany, so it will take further structural changes in the market before stripping really takes off," he said. "But it will happen over time."
Pension funds have a particular penchant for strips because they can match specific assets and liabilities.
Analysts said this would show through in demand for certain coupons, where funds who know the timing and amount of pension payouts can hedge them in the strips market.

Mat Knowles, bond strategist at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said Bund strips were experiencing some teething problems, but had had a good start and looked set to grow in popularity and depth once those problems are ironed out.
"It will probably take a year or so before the liquidity squeezes we're seeing at the moment disappear," he said, noting in particular a squeeze from high demand in 30-year maturities.

"But with the French market becoming more established, Germany getting that way in a couple of years, Spain intending to introduce strips either this year or next, and Britain's strip market due to start this year, we'll soon have a whole new market across Europe," he said.
